points.description: Sets up a proof by contradiction (assume all roots of P are real, so distinct real) and reduces to n=k+1 by taking a degree-(k+1) factor of P (product of k+1 of the linear factors). Its divisors are also divisors of P and it keeps nonzero constant term and distinct real roots. A student who handles general n directly with a valid argument also earns this.

For n=k+1, the degree-k divisors are Q_i=P/(x-r_i), i=1..n. The leading and constant coefficients of each Q_i are nonzero, so the hypothesis forces a zero coefficient at some position j in {1,...,k-1}. Since there are k+1 divisors and only k-1 positions, pigeonhole gives two different divisors Q_r, Q_s with a zero coefficient at the same position j. (k=1 case: no interior positions, so contradiction is immediate.)

levels.says: Notes that a zero coefficient must be interior, or counts divisors versus positions, but does not complete the pigeonhole to a common position.

points.description: Writes R=P/((x-r)(x-s)), which has degree k-1 and distinct real roots with nonzero constant term. Uses Q_r=(x-s)R and Q_s=(x-r)R. Obtains from the shared zero at position j either Q_r-Q_s=(s-r)R (so R_j=0) and then the zero coefficient of Q_r gives R_{j-1}-sR_j=0, so R_{j-1}=0. Concludes R has two consecutive zero coefficients (positions j-1 and j). Any equivalent derivation is accepted.

levels.says: Introduces R or a similar polynomial but does not correctly derive two consecutive zero coefficients.
Shows one zero coefficient of R, or gets two consecutive zeros with a minor algebra slip.

points.description: Proves that a polynomial with only distinct real roots and nonzero constant term cannot have two consecutive zero coefficients. Valid proofs: differentiate j-1 times (Rolle keeps all roots real and distinct) to get a polynomial with zero constant and zero linear term, hence a double root at 0, which is a contradiction. Newton's inequalities or Descartes' rule of signs, correctly applied, are also accepted. Merely asserting the claim without justification earns at most 0.5.

levels.says: Gives the right idea (derivatives or Newton/Descartes) but with a gap, such as not justifying distinct real roots after differentiation or mishandling the edge case.

rubric.notes: Full marks need the full argument: reduction to n=k+1, the pigeonhole giving two divisors with a common zero position, the two consecutive zero coefficients of R, and the proof that this is impossible for a polynomial with distinct real roots. The official partial credit corresponds to P2 (shared zero position) and to finding a real-rooted polynomial with two consecutive zero coefficients (P3). A correct alternative method earns equivalent marks. Proofs that assume the claim in P4 without justification lose most of P4.
rubric.answer_key: Suppose all roots of P are real (hence distinct). Take any k+1 of them; their linear factors multiply to a degree-(k+1) divisor of P, so WLOG n=k+1. The degree-k divisors Q_i=P/(x-r_i) (i=1..n) have nonzero constant and leading coefficients (r_i≠0 since P(0)≠0). By hypothesis each has a zero coefficient at some position in 1..k-1. There are k+1 divisors and k-1 positions, so two divisors Q_r, Q_s (r≠s) have zero coefficients at the same position j. Let R=P/((x-r)(x-s)), of degree k-1. Then Q_r=(x-s)R and Q_s=(x-r)R, so Q_r-Q_s=(r-s)R. Hence the coefficient R_j=0. The x^j coefficient of Q_r is R_{j-1}-sR_j=0, so R_{j-1}=0. So R has two consecutive zero coefficients, but R has distinct real roots and R(0)≠0. Differentiate R (j-1) times. The result still has only distinct real roots (Rolle), but its constant and linear terms are both 0, so 0 is a double root. This is a contradiction. Hence P has a non-real root.
